Thanks, Chloe — appreciate the clear recap. Quick answers and a few clarifications: 

- Current provider: we’re on VectorCloud (vendor) using 1024-d float32 embeddings. We currently do per-item requests from our search layer (no batching at client side) and a nightly job that reindexes 10M docs.
- Normalization: we normalize with L2 on write in the existing pipeline, so scores today are cosine-similarity-based.
- Desired change: we are open to reducing to 768 if you recommend it, but we’d like to understand the expected quality delta for our reranker (we use a pairwise reranker downstream).
- Auth: for now we prefer API keys for the POC; long term we will likely move to OIDC via our IdP.

Hi Anna / Samuel / Chloe —

Thanks for the sample confirmation, Anna. Some technical guidance ahead of the deep-dive so we can focus on the migration playbook: 

1) Dimension decision (1024 -> 768):
- Tradeoffs: 768 will typically reduce token and compute cost ~25-35% depending on runtime kernels; some open models (and our optimized quantized variants) offer near-parity for semantic search at 768.
- Recommendation: run an A/B quality check on a 5k sample. If pairwise reranker downstream is sensitive, we recommend preserving 1024 for the POC and running a background experiment that generates 768 vectors to compare NDCG/recall.

2) Normalization & scoring:
- Keep L2 normalization on write if you rely on cosine similarity. Redwood supports both normalized vectors (dot product) and raw vectors with inline normalization.
- If you switch to dot-product on unnormalized vectors, we’ll need to update the reranker scoring to account for magnitude differences. Simpler: continue L2 norm and use dot-product.

3) Batching and throughput:
- Client-side batching: target batching of 32-128 vectors per request depending on your latency SLO. For synchronous user queries, prefer smaller batches (~16-32). For bulk indexing, use large batches (256-1024) with parallel workers.
- On the Redwood side we recommend 'dynamic batching' in the SDK; default good starting point: max_batch_items=256, max_latency_ms=25.

4) Migration strategy (zero-downtime approach):
- Phase 1: Dual-write for new content (write both existing provider and Redwood vectors).
- Phase 2: Background reindex: spawn workers to read existing doc store, compute Redwood vectors, and write to new index. Use a feature flag to control read path.
- Phase 3: Canary reads: route X% of live queries to Redwood vectors and compare scores / user metrics.
- Phase 4: Cutover once metrics are within acceptable delta.

5) SDK & auth snippet (high level):
- SDK initialize: redwood = RedwoodClient(api_key="<REDACTED>", region="us-west-2")
- Batch call example: redwood.embeddings.create_batch(model="rwd-embed-768", inputs=[...], normalize=true)
- For OIDC flows we support token exchange with short-lived tokens; we can provide example code in auth-snippets.txt.

6) Reranker compatibility:
- If your reranker expects 1024 input vectors, we can either: (a) retrain small head to accept 768, (b) keep reranker unchanged and use a model that preserves 1024. Retraining is recommended if you make the dim change.

Attachments I’m leaving: batching-recommendations.pdf is a quick table of throughput numbers we’ve observed across GPUs. I’ll bring more concrete numbers to Thu’s deep dive.

Happy to expand on any item in the call.
